sub: The heart of the Syro-Malankara Church: what it is, how it unfolds, and how to take part
sec: What the word means

“Qurbono” is the West Syriac form of the Syriac word qurbānā (in the East Syriac pronunciation, Qurbana). It comes from the root q-r-b, “to draw near” and “to offer”. The Holy Qurbono is the offering by which Christ draws near to us and we are drawn near to the Father.

It is not simply a prayer meeting or a devotion. It is the Eucharistic sacrifice: the one sacrifice of Christ on the Cross made present, in which bread and wine become truly, really and substantially his Body and Blood, and are given to us as food for eternal life.
Its roots

The Syro-Malankara Church celebrates the Holy Qurbono in the West Syriac (Antiochene) tradition, the liturgy of the ancient Church of Antioch and Jerusalem. Its principal anaphora (Eucharistic prayer) bears the name of St James, “the brother of the Lord” and first bishop of Jerusalem; the Church also uses other approved anaphoras.

When Archbishop Mar Ivanios entered full communion with the Catholic Church in 1930, this liturgy was kept whole. The Catholic Church treasures it: the Eastern Churches are of equal dignity with the Latin Church and are asked to preserve their own rites (Orientalium Ecclesiarum 3, 6).
How it unfolds

1. Preparation. Before the public celebration the priest prepares the altar, the bread and the wine (mixed with a little water), with prayers of humility. The bread is leavened, as in the Syriac tradition.

2. The opening and the Word. The veil of the sanctuary is opened and the celebration begins with incense and hymns. The Trisagion (“Holy are you, O God…”) is sung. Readings from the Apostles are proclaimed, then the Gospel (Evangelion), heard standing. The Sedro, a long prayer with incense, asks forgiveness and blessing. The Nicene Creed is professed.

3. The Anaphora. The peace (Shlomo) is passed from the altar through the people: we are reconciled before we offer. The priest invites: “Let our minds, our thoughts and our hearts be on high”, and all sing the Sanctus. He recalls the Last Supper and repeats Christ's words over the bread and the cup. Then comes the Epiclesis: the Holy Spirit is called down upon the gifts and upon the people, and the people answer “Kurielaison” three times. In the great intercessions (Thubden) the Church remembers the living and the dead, the Mother of God, the saints and the fathers.

4. Communion. The Lord's Prayer is said. The priest breaks the Holy Body and unites it with the Blood. He lifts the Mysteries: “Holy things for the holy.” The faithful receive the Body dipped in the Blood (intinction). After communion come thanksgiving, the final blessing and the dismissal; the priest bids farewell to the altar with a moving prayer that he may return to it in peace.
What the Church believes
It is a true sacrifice: not a new sacrifice, but the one sacrifice of the Cross made present, so that its fruits are applied to us (CCC 1366–1367).

Christ is truly present under the appearances of bread and wine, whole and entire, Body and Blood, soul and divinity; this change the Church calls transubstantiation (CCC 1374–1376; Council of Trent).
The Holy Spirit makes the gifts holy. Eastern liturgies give great emphasis to the Epiclesis, the invocation of the Spirit (CCC 1353).
It is the action of the whole Church, Head and members, on earth and in heaven, united with the Pope and the bishops, whose names are remembered at the altar.
How to take part well

Come before it begins; the prayers of the beginning belong to you too. Stand when the Church stands; it is the posture of the risen. Answer aloud and sing. Follow the actions: incense, veil, peace, elevation; each speaks.
Receive Holy Communion with faith and reverence, having kept the Eucharistic fast laid down by the Church. After the Qurbono, stay for the thanksgiving; then live what you received.
The sanctuary and its signs

In a Syro-Malankara church the sanctuary (Madbaho) is raised and separated from the nave by a curtain. The curtain is opened and closed at fixed moments: closed during the preparation, opened at the beginning of the public celebration, closed again at moments of great mystery. It teaches that the Holy Qurbono is the opening of heaven to us, and that we approach it with awe.

On the altar lies the tablitho, a consecrated board on which the Mysteries are celebrated. Liturgical fans with small bells (marvahtho), shaped like the wings of the seraphim, are waved over the gifts, recalling the angels who surround the throne of God (Isaiah 6:2). The censer, with its little bells, is used often: the incense rises like prayer (Psalm 141:2).
Vestments and gestures

The priest wears the kuthino (white tunic), the hamnikho (stole), the zenoro (girdle), the zendo (cuffs) and the phayno (the large outer vestment, like a cope). The deacon wears an orarion over the shoulder. Each vestment is put on with a prayer.

The people make the sign of the Cross often, bow at the Trisagion and at the blessing, answer “Kurielaison” and sing the hymns. At the peace, the peace passes hand to hand from the altar through the whole congregation: Christ's peace comes from the altar, not from ourselves.
Questions people ask

Why is the curtain drawn? Not to hide the Mysteries from the people, but to express their holiness. Moses removed his sandals before the burning bush (Exodus 3:5); the curtain teaches the same reverence.
Why are the prayers sung? The West Syriac tradition believes that the Church on earth joins the song of the angels. Singing makes the prayer the prayer of all.
Why Communion by intinction? The Holy Body is dipped in the Holy Blood and given with a spoon or by the priest's hand, so that the faithful receive the Lord under both kinds.
How often may I receive? Every day if properly disposed; a second time on the same day only within a Holy Qurbono in which you take part.
notes: Anyone conscious of grave (mortal) sin must receive the sacrament of Confession before receiving Holy Communion (CCC 1385; 1 Corinthians 11:27–29).
Participation in the Holy Qurbono on Sundays and holy days of obligation is a grave duty of every Catholic, unless excused for a serious reason such as illness or the care of infants (CCC 2180–2181).
Catholics should receive Communion only in Catholic celebrations, except in the specific cases foreseen by Church law (CCC 1398–1401).
The liturgy belongs to the Church, not to any individual: no priest or community may add, remove or change anything on its own authority (Sacrosanctum Concilium 22).
Treat the consecrated Body and Blood with the utmost care; no particle should fall or be left behind.
The Eucharistic fast before Holy Communion is laid down by the particular law of each Church sui iuris; follow the current norm of the Syro-Malankara Church (CCEO c. 713 §2).
refs: Second Vatican Council, Sacrosanctum Concilium 47–48; Orientalium Ecclesiarum 1–6

sub: How the Syro-Malankara Church walks through the mystery of Christ in seven seasons, from the Sanctification of the Church to the Holy Cross
sec: Why a liturgical year?

Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8), yet in the course of a year the Church unfolds his whole mystery, from the announcement of his birth to his coming again, so that we may enter it step by step and be transformed (CCC 1163–1171).

The West Syriac tradition, which the Syro-Malankara Church received from Antioch, sings the year more than it explains it. Its hymns (madrashe and qolo) for each Sunday lead the faithful through the events of salvation, so that each season becomes a school of prayer.
Sunday and the date of Qyomtho

Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, is the foundation and heart of the whole year. Each Sunday has its own readings, usually from the Old Testament, the Acts or Catholic Epistles, St Paul and the Gospel, and its own hymns.

The most important feast is Qyomtho (Easter). Its date follows the rule of the Council of Nicaea: the Sunday after the first full moon after the spring equinox. Many other days depend on it: the Nineveh fast, the Great Fast, Sulokho (the Ascension, on the fortieth day) and Pentecost (the fiftieth day). Because the date of Qyomtho moves, the number of Sundays after Denho and after Pentecost changes from year to year.
1. Suboro: the season of announcements

The year begins with two Sundays that look at the Church herself: Qudos Eetho, the Sanctification of the Church, and Hudos Eetho, the Dedication of the Church. Before celebrating the coming of Christ, the Church remembers what she is: the holy dwelling of God among his people.

Then come the Sundays of the announcements, which follow the Gospel of Luke and Matthew: the annunciation to Zechariah, the annunciation to Mary, the visitation of Mary to Elizabeth, the birth of John the Baptist, the revelation to Joseph, and the Sunday before Yaldo with the genealogy of the Lord. The Twenty-Five Days' Fast (1–25 December) accompanies these weeks.
2. Yaldo and Denho: the birth and manifestation of the Lord

Yaldo, the Birth of the Lord (25 December), opens the season of the Nativity. The Sundays after Yaldo remember the flight into Egypt and the childhood of Christ; on 1 January the Church keeps the Naming and Circumcision of the Lord.

Denho (6 January) celebrates the Baptism of the Lord in the Jordan and the manifestation of the Holy Trinity. Its liturgy includes the solemn blessing of water. The Sundays after Denho remember the witness of John the Baptist and the beginning of the Lord's ministry; before the Great Fast come the Sunday of the Priests (Kohne) and the Sunday of the Faithful Departed (Aneede). Mayaltho, the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple, is kept on 2 February. The Three Days' (Nineveh) Fast is kept in the weeks before the Great Fast.
3. The Great Fast and the week of the Passion

The Great Fast begins on Shubkono, the Monday of reconciliation, when the faithful ask forgiveness of one another before entering the fast. The Sunday before it is Kothine, the wedding at Cana: Christ who changed water into wine will change us.

The Sundays of the fast are named after the healings of the Lord: Garbo (the leper), Mshario (the paralytic), Knanoitho (the Canaanite woman), Kpiphtho (the bent woman) and Samio (the blind man). The middle of the fast is marked on its Wednesday; the fortieth Friday closes the forty days, followed by the Saturday of Lazarus.

Hosanna Sunday opens the week of the Passion. On Pesaha Thursday the Church celebrates the Last Supper with the washing of the feet; on Good Friday the long service of the Passion, with the veneration and burial of the Cross; on Holy Saturday the Church keeps vigil at the tomb. The period from the beginning of the Great Fast to the first Sunday after Pentecost is called the Season of the Passover.
4–7. Qyomtho, Pentecost, Transfiguration and the Holy Cross

4. Qyomtho. The Resurrection is the feast of feasts, celebrated in the night with the proclamation of the risen Lord and the service of peace. The New Sunday follows, with the Gospel of St Thomas; Sulokho, the Ascension, is kept on the fortieth day.

5. Pentecost. The coming of the Holy Spirit is celebrated with the special prayers of kneeling, in which the Church asks the Spirit to come upon her as upon the apostles. The Sundays after Pentecost show the life of the Church in the Spirit; Sts Peter and Paul (29 June) and the Dukrono of St Thomas (3 July) fall in this season, and on 15 July the Church remembers Mar Ivanios.

6. Transfiguration (M'thale, 6 August). Christ's glory on the mountain gives hope in suffering. The Shunoyo, the falling asleep and assumption of Mary (15 August), and her Nativity (8 September) fall in this season.

7. Sleebo (the Holy Cross, 14 September). The last season of the year looks at the Cross and at the end of time: the sign of the Son of Man, the judgment and the Second Coming of Christ. The Reunion Day (20 September) recalls the entry of Mar Ivanios and his companions into full communion with the Catholic Church in 1930.
The great feasts

Feasts of the Lord: Yaldo, Denho, Mayaltho (2 February), Qyomtho, Sulokho, Pentecost and M'thale. Observed like feasts of the Lord: Suboro (the Annunciation, 25 March), Sts Peter and Paul (29 June), the Dukrono of St Thomas (3 July), the Shunoyo (15 August) and the Holy Cross (14 September).
On these days, and on every Sunday, the faithful take part in the Holy Qurbono, refrain from servile work and keep the day holy with Scripture, prayer and good works.
Fasts (Nombu)
Canonical fasts: the Twenty-Five Days' Fast (1–25 December), the Three Days' (Nineveh) Fast, and the Fifty Days' Great Fast.

Pious fasts, recommended though not binding by law: the Thirteen Days' Fast of the Apostles (before 29 June), the Fifteen Days' Fast before the Shunoyo (1–15 August) and the Eight Days' Fast before the Nativity of Mary (1–8 September). Many also keep the Mar Ivanios fast (1–15 July) for the cause of the Servant of God.
In the Syriac tradition fasting is joined to prayer at the canonical hours, to reconciliation and to almsgiving. A fast that leaves the heart hard has missed its purpose (Isaiah 58:6–7).
Living the year at home

Learn the name of each Sunday and read its Gospel at home on Saturday evening. Keep the fasts as a family, with simpler meals and gifts to the poor. Ask forgiveness of one another on Shubkono; keep silence and prayer on Good Friday; greet one another with the joy of the Resurrection at Qyomtho.
Teach children the meaning of the great feasts and of the saints of our Church. When the rhythm of the Church enters the home, the family becomes a little church.
notes: On all Fridays and on the days of the Twenty-Five Days', Three Days' and Great Fasts, the faithful abstain from meat. The days between the Nineveh fast and the Great Fast, and the fifty days from Qyomtho to Pentecost, are exempt.

On the days of the Nineveh fast, on Shubkono and on the Fridays of the Great Fast, and from the fortieth Friday to Qyomtho, the faithful also abstain from fish and eggs; on Good Friday also from milk and milk products. There is no abstinence on the closing day of a fast.
All are obliged to take part in the special services of Good Friday; on Maundy Thursday all, young and old, should take part in the Holy Qurbono and receive worthily.
Those who are sick, pregnant or nursing, the elderly and those doing heavy work should consult their pastor; fasting must never endanger health (cf. CCC 2043).
These rules follow the Syro-Malankara Sacred Lectionary; always follow the current circular of your eparchy.

The Syro-Malankara Church uses the liturgy of St James in the West Syriac tradition; its calendar and hymns differ from the East Syriac (Syro-Malabar) and Roman calendars, though the great feasts are shared.
refs: Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, The Sacred Lectionary (introduction: feasts, fasts, abstinence, liturgical year)

sub: Why we confess, how to examine our conscience, how to make a good confession, and what the Church asks of us
sec: Christ gave this sacrament

On the evening of Easter the risen Lord breathed on the apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). Through the bishops and priests, their successors, Christ continues to forgive sins in the Church (CCC 1441–1445).

This sacrament has many names: conversion, penance, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation (CCC 1423–1424). In Kerala we usually say “Kumbasaram”. It is the sacrament of the prodigal son coming home and of the Father who runs to embrace him (Luke 15:20).
Why confess to a priest?

Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). But God chose to forgive through his Church: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive and to retain, which they could not use without hearing the sins (CCC 1461–1462). The priest is not a judge who condemns but a minister of mercy who acts in the person of Christ, the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep (CCC 1465).

Sin is never purely private. It wounds the Body of Christ, the Church. So reconciliation with God is also reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445, 1469). Hearing the words of absolution spoken aloud gives a certainty of forgiveness that our feelings alone cannot give.
Mortal and venial sin

Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart: it is a sin whose object is grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments. Mortal sin, unless repented and forgiven, separates us from God for ever (CCC 1861).

Venial sin weakens charity but does not destroy it (CCC 1862–1863). Confessing everyday faults is strongly recommended: it helps us form our conscience, fight evil tendencies, let ourselves be healed by Christ and grow in the life of the Spirit (CCC 1458).
Examining the conscience

An honest examination is the first step. Some questions, following the Commandments: Do I pray daily? Have I denied my faith or been ashamed of it? Have I used God's name carelessly or sworn falsely? Have I missed the Holy Qurbana or Mass on Sundays and days of obligation without serious reason?

Have I honoured my parents and cared for them? Have I been unjust, violent or harsh at home, at work, with servants or employees? Have I harmed life: by anger, hatred, abortion, abuse of alcohol or drugs, reckless driving? Have I sinned against chastity in thought, word or deed, alone or with others, through pornography? Have I been faithful in marriage?

Have I stolen, cheated, taken bribes, failed to pay just wages or debts, wasted money while others are in need? Have I lied, gossiped, ruined another's good name, posted harmful things on social media? Have I been envious, greedy, proud, lazy in my duties? Have I neglected the poor?

Children and young people can ask more simply: Did I pray? Did I obey my parents and teachers? Did I tell lies, fight, use bad words, take what is not mine, cheat in exams, waste time on the phone, hurt anyone?
The three acts of the penitent

1. Contrition: sorrow of soul and hatred for the sin committed, with the resolution not to sin again. Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect contrition (attrition) comes from fear of punishment or the ugliness of sin, and is sufficient for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

2. Confession: telling the priest all mortal sins of which, after careful examination, we are conscious, with their kind and number, as far as we can (CCC 1456). Speak simply and honestly; there is no need for long stories or for naming other people.

3. Satisfaction: doing the penance the priest gives, to repair the harm and restore our habits as disciples of Christ (CCC 1459–1460). Where we have harmed others, we must also make it right: return what was taken, restore a damaged reputation, ask forgiveness.
How to make a good confession
Before: pray to the Holy Spirit for light; examine your conscience; awaken sorrow by looking at the crucifix and remembering God's love.

In the confessional: make the sign of the Cross; say how long it has been since your last confession and, if helpful, your state of life (married, student, priest or religious); confess your sins; listen to the priest's counsel and accept the penance; pray an act of contrition; receive absolution with faith. In the Eastern Churches the prayer of absolution often asks God to forgive the penitent; in the Latin Church the priest says “I absolve you”. Both are true and valid forms of the same sacrament.

A traditional act of contrition: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you, and I detest all my sins because of your just punishments, but most of all because they offend you, my God, who are all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of your grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. (Any approved act of contrition may be used, such as the one taught in your parish catechism.)
After: thank God; do the penance soon; repair any harm done; avoid the occasions of sin; come back regularly, not only when burdened by grave sin.
What the sacrament gives

Reconciliation with God, by which grace is restored; reconciliation with the Church; remission of the eternal punishment due to mortal sin and, at least in part, of temporal punishment; peace and serenity of conscience and spiritual consolation; and an increase of strength for the Christian battle (CCC 1468–1470, 1496).

Many people find that the hardest step is the first one, the walk to the confessional. Beyond it is the joy of the Father: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).
Children, first confession and frequent confession

Children who have reached the age of discretion (around seven) are prepared for their first confession before their first Holy Communion (CCC 1457; c. 914). Parents should go with them and confess themselves; children learn most from what they see.

The saints recommend confessing regularly, for example monthly, and before the great feasts. Many parishes offer confession during the Twenty-Five Days' Fast and the Great Fast or Lent; make use of these times.
notes: Every Catholic who has reached the age of discretion must confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042, 1457).

One who is conscious of mortal sin must not receive Holy Communion without first going to confession, except when there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess; then an act of perfect contrition must be made, with the intention of confessing as soon as possible (CCC 1457, 1385).

Deliberately hiding a mortal sin in confession makes the confession invalid and adds the sin of sacrilege; the hidden sin and the sacrilege must be confessed. Forgetting a sin is not hiding it: the forgotten sin is forgiven and should be mentioned at the next confession.
The priest is bound by the absolute seal of confession: he may never reveal or use what he hears, under the most severe penalties (CCC 1467; Code of Canon Law c. 983; CCEO c. 733).
Absolution requires real contrition and the purpose of amendment; it cannot be given to one who refuses to give up a grave sin or to repair a grave injustice.

General absolution without individual confession is allowed only in grave necessity (danger of death, or very large numbers with no possibility of individual confession for a long time); grave sins must then be confessed individually as soon as possible (CCC 1483).
Some very grave sins carry penalties whose remission is reserved; if this concerns you, speak to a priest, who will explain the path of reconciliation.
refs: Code of Canon Law cc. 959–991; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches cc. 718–736
